definition: Arabic renders right-to-left, and real text mixes RTL words with LTR numerals, code, and English terms, governed by the Unicode Bidi algorithm.
details: Arabic renders right-to-left, and real text mixes RTL words with LTR numerals, code, and English terms, governed by the Unicode Bidi algorithm. A perennial source of UI bugs, corrupted string concatenation, and mangled LLM outputs when markup and directional marks are handled carelessly.

explainer.lead: Right-to-left scripts such as Arabic mix with left-to-right numerals, code, and English terms, and the Unicode Bidi algorithm governs how the mixture is ordered. It matters because careless handling causes UI bugs, corrupted string concatenation, and mangled LLM output.

tiers.eli5: Arabic reads right to left, but a phone number inside an Arabic sentence still reads left to right, so software has to juggle two directions in one line.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on the Unicode Bidi algorithm and directional marks when rendering and concatenating mixed-direction strings. A pitfall is building strings by naive concatenation of markup and text, which reorders or corrupts displayed output.
tiers.paperLevel: The Unicode Bidi algorithm assigns characters directional types and resolves display order through an explicit rule sequence; correctness depends on applying it consistently, and mixing raw markup or unmarked numerals breaks the expected order.

explainer.example: An Arabic sentence containing a version number like 'v2.0' displays reversed unless the numeral run is isolated with directional marks.
